questions.question: In a metric space $(\boldsymbol{X},d_{\boldsymbol{X}})$, what does it mean for $\boldsymbol{E}\subseteq\boldsymbol{X}$ to be bounded?
options: Every ball in $\boldsymbol{X}$ contains $\boldsymbol{E}$.
$\boldsymbol{E}$ contains every ball centred at each of its points.
$\boldsymbol{E}$ has no points outside the origin.
There exists $M \gt 0$ such that some ball $\boldsymbol{B}_{(\boldsymbol{X},d_{\boldsymbol{X}})}(\boldsymbol{x},M)$ contains $\boldsymbol{E}$.
questions.explanation: A set is bounded if it can be contained within some ball of finite radius. The centre can be any point of $X$; the key requirement is that one such ball exists.
questions.source_support: The definition states that $\boldsymbol{E}$ is bounded if it is contained in a ball of radius $M \gt 0$.
questions.polish_notes: Quality round 9: rebalanced correct-answer positions to remove option-index guessing cue
option_explanations: Requiring every ball to contain $E$ is far too strong; we only need that at least one ball of finite radius contains $E$.
Containing every ball centred at each of its points would make $E$ the whole space, not bounded.
Boundedness has nothing to do with an origin; many metric spaces have no distinguished origin.

option_explanations: A set containing every point of the metric space is the whole space, which is typically unbounded.
A set with no open metric balls inside it is unrelated to boundedness; many bounded sets contain open balls.
Bounded sets need not be spheres; any shape that fits in some ball is bounded.
